query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of aluminum (on the order of 2–5 atomic percent) to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will improve its oxygen resistance by promoting the formation of a continuous, protective alumina (Al2O3) scale on the alloy surface during high-temperature exposure.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy that exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strengths in the range of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by alloying with approximately 2–5 at.% aluminum.
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at temperatures between 800 °C and 1000 °C, for durations comparable to or longer than 5 hours and under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹, similar to previous oxidation and mechanical tests.
generation.structural_mediator: The in situ formation of a dense, adherent alumina (Al2O3) scale on the alloy’s surface.
generation.mechanism: During high-temperature exposure in air, the added aluminum preferentially oxidizes at the surface to form a thin, continuous alumina layer. This scale acts as a barrier that slows oxygen diffusion into the material, thereby reducing overall oxidation rates while preserving the alloy’s bulk microstructure and mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Al-doped alloy will demonstrate significantly reduced oxygen uptake and surface degradation compared to the untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, while maintaining similar room-temperature tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr shows 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength ranging between 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but suffers from inadequate oxygen resistance.
generation.boundary: Effectiveness is anticipated for exposures in air at high temperatures (800–1000 °C) for at least 5 hours under low strain rate conditions; the intervention must not adversely alter the phase prior or mechanical performance under typical loading conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal aluminum concentration and its impact on phase stability and mechanical properties require further tuning. It is uncertain whether the minimal addition will affect other alloy characteristics, and the long-term adhesion and integrity of the alumina scale under cyclic thermal/mechanical conditions also remain to be evaluated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one group of conventional equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and another group modified with 2–5 at.% Al. Subject both groups to oxidation in an air atmosphere at 800 °C for 5 hours while maintaining similar strain rates. After exposure, analyze the material surfaces and cross-sections using microscopy (e.g., SEM/TEM) for the presence and continuity of a protective oxide layer, and perform weight gain measurements to quantify oxygen uptake. Conduct mechanical tests at room temperature and 1000 °C to evaluate tensile ductility and yield strength.
measurements: Surface and cross-sectional microstructural analysis (SEM/TEM) to confirm the alumina scale formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminum-modified samples fail to form a continuous and protective alumina layer, do not show a reduction in oxygen uptake compared to the untreated samples, or if the intervention significantly degrades the mechanical properties (e.g., marked reduction in tensile ductility or yield strength), then the hypothesis is falsified.

Effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on Mechanical Properties of Equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr Alloys

Abstract: AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect

Conclusions: The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen
